own_scenes.desc: A principios de 1966 había tres programas pop. Top of the Pops (BBC1) presentaba la lista tal cual, de Eddy Arnold a los Stones; A Whole Scene Going (BBC2), con Barry Fantoni y Wendy Varnals, era más reflexivo. El mejor era Ready Steady Go! (agosto de 1963-1966), que traducía al televisor el ritmo de la cultura juvenil: actuaciones en directo entre el público, mujeres como presentadoras, productoras y artistas (Vicki Wickham, Cathy McGowan), visitantes de Tamla y del soul, y la cámara de Michael Lindsay-Hogg pegada a Jagger y a las bailarinas mod de falda corta. En agosto de 1965 el público invadió el plató mientras los Stones tocaban «Satisfaction».

notes.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia
notes.text: Rediffusion canceló Ready Steady Go! en noviembre por caro; el último programa se emitió el 23 de diciembre de 1966. Para Tony Hall su misión estaba cumplida: sin él no habría triunfado el soul americano ni la revolución de la moda británica. «Toda la emoción se ha ido», dijo Vicki Wickham.

refs.q: The best show of all was Ready Steady Go!
refs.para: The best show of all was Ready Steady Go!, a sharply conceived, fast-running weekly programme that aimed to translate the excitement of pop and the pace of youth culture directly through the screen, as Jack Good’s Oh Boy! had in the late 1950s. Beginning in August 1963 and continuing through into 1966, it featured all the major groups of the day, along with significant American visitors – most notably soul and Tamla acts – as well as promoting women as presenters, producers and artists.
refs.chapter: Febrero: 19th Nervous Breakdown: la cultura adolescente británica y la locura del Swinging London

refs.q: In mid-November, Rediffusion announced the cancellation of Ready Steady Go!
refs.para: In mid-November, Rediffusion announced the cancellation of Ready Steady Go!, which was seen as too expensive for the ratings it attracted. The weekly programme had been an integral part of the broadcasting and development of Britain’s youth music since its inception in early August 1963. As Vicki Wickham reminded the readers of Disc and Music Echo, it had featured the Beatles, very early appearances by the Rolling Stones, the Animals and Dusty Springfield, and US visitors like Ike and Tina Turner, ‘who came over better than anything else we’ve done’.
